Title: The Object of Jyhad (Was R. Goudie's Prey and "Cheese" Threads)

Messages.Author: Richard Zopf
Messages.Body:
To Alll,
Doesn't it strike you as interesting that the arguments bandied about
regarding whether particular deck stratefies are "cheesy" or not seems to
depend on a difference in what the two arguers see as the goal of a
tournament?
Some players regard creativity to be of a greater inportance than
absolute performance in a tournament. They're most happy with a strong
blend of the two (they typically object to weenie Misdirect, either on the
grounds that it is too effective, inelegant, unoriginal, or unchallenging to
play.)
Others want to win tournaments. They see the greatest satisfaction in a
tournament to come from playing as absolutely cutthroat as possible. If
their opponents aren't doing the same, then they see those opponents as
deserving to lose. Any notion of a tournament being for another purpose
seems absurd to them. (Know which category you belong to yet?)

The Cheese Debate(tm) stems from a fundamental difference in what the
two competitor types are trying to achieve. Most times this difference is
rooted in the habits of the gaming group to which the member belongs.
Contrast attitudes from LA players (Robert Goudie & Jedi Mike)looking for
raw victory points, to those of the Southeast (Atlanta: Davila, Pieloch; New
Orleans: Sorrow, etc.) looking for creative satisfaction in addition to
victory points. Their gaming groups use tournaments for different ends.
Their peers measure "tournament success" by different scales, and as such
either support "cheesy" decks or reject them, based on whether they assist
in meeting the reasons for having a tournament in the first place...
Can the two be happy in the same tournament? Probably not without a
dynamic environment, in which the introduction of new cards causes a
continuous shift in tournament dynamic (we all hope for that). The only
other way to make both happy is to shift tournament category (I'd bet Robert
Goudie and Sorrow would have a great time at a sealed or draft tournament
together) or change the base rules of the game (as in a variant
environmental rules structure, which I would _not_ advocate).

I'm sure this is only one aspect of The Cheese Debate(tm), but I think
it's an important one... Your thoughts, comments, etc.???

--
Regards,
R. David Zopf
Atom Weaver (& V:EKN Prince of Charlotte, NC)

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
David Zopf wrote:
<<Others want to win tournaments. They see the greatest satisfaction in a
tournament to come from playing as absolutely cutthroat as possible. If
their opponents aren't doing the same, then they see those opponents as
deserving to lose. Any notion of a tournament being for another purpose
seems absurd to them. (Know which category you belong to yet?)>>

I really don't think it as cut and dry as you are making it out here. I, who am
arguing for what would appear to be the "must win at any cost" camp simply does
not fit into that world view.

I love playing Jyhad, and while I always enjoy winning, it is not the be all
and end all of the game for me. If I lose, so what? I don 't play particularly
cut throat, nor do I play particularly "cheesy" decks (i.e. I very rarely, if
ever, play weenie misdirect bleed decks, or weenie vote, or anything of the
sort). I don't play Jyhad to win at any cost, nor do any of my cohorts, which
is what you seem to be implying by the above statement (this isn't a
disgruntled reply, I'm just examining your point). We do not play to crush our
enemies and laugh at them because they lose under my mighty heel. That isn't
the point.

The concept that I am defending is that of competetition for competition's
sake. Jyhad is, as I point out on a regular basis, a competetive game, with
very well defined rules for winning. As such, if you aren't playing with
winning as a major motivation, you are ommiting a major part of the structure
of the game, and as such, it starts to collapse.

Again--I am neither cutthroat, vicious, or mocking of my opponents. I just
enjoy playing Jyhad in a situation where I and my opponents are all operating
under the same rules set, and that rules set involves trying to win the game.
If this means that people are going to use "cheesy" decks, so be it--more power
to them, and I'm not going to begrudge them their victory for it. I'm just
going to try and build decks that can compete, and win, against them.

And if I lose? Who cares. We play again. And If I lose that game? We play
again. The point is not the victory--the point is the effort and the attempt.
If I'm not trying to win, I am shorting my opponents and they are not going to
have fun. If they aren't trying to win, I'm not going to have fun.

Peter D Bakija

Richard,

The world is made up of two kinds of kinds of people: people who attempt
to classify the world into two kinds and people who don't.

I think you're pretty much missing the boat in your attempts to put this
whole argument down to a simple difference of objective. For one thing,
I don't agree with this whole cheese-deck thing at all, yet I have no
desire whatsoever to find the best deck and limit myself to it. I don't
think I fit anywhere in your world view. To me, tournaments are mainly
fun because you're guranteed multiple games in the same day. And with
new opponents, no less.

The problem with your theory is that it assumes people are arguing for
something based on what they want. The assumption you made in your first
paragraph is frequently wrong: many people do *NOT* form their opinion of
whether a deck is "cheesy" or not based on whether they view creativity or
winning tournaments as more imporant. In fact, IMHO, the more significant
difference between the view points has a lot more to do with the different
peoples' ideas of what an "imaginative" deck actually is. Some people seem
to think that anything they can imagine that wins games differently than
the popular ("cheesy") decks is imaginative. I suppose it is on some level,
but if you don't take effectiveness into account, you're basically trying
to win by _hoping_ some given idea will work and then blaming the opponents
if it doesn't in real life. I guess I think of an "imaginative" deck as
one that actually uses an imaginative response to solving the _real_
problems of playing Jyhad - including what to do when you encounter a
weeny bleed preditor with Misdirection.

So no, the Cheese Debate does not stem from what people are trying to
acheive, IMHO. It stems from differing ideas about what it means to use
your imagination: just to think up a new combination of cards, or to think
one up that works at solving the problems a deck will enounter in a game.

Fred

I find this to be a very interesting point. There was mention above that
many thematic players are "superlative players" which I snipped because
I thought I'd mention it. The guy that got me started is a very
supurlative player, and quite thematic (probably one of the reasons I
play the way I do.)

I find it interesting that the term "Cliche' deck" is used above, and
perhaps we should substitute Cliche for Cheese as it seems more
appropriate. <<more on this below>>

I first encountered Jyhad several years ago at a local card shop after
being frustratingly ousted from a M:TG tournament by some 10 year olds
with card collections exceeding my annual salary. (No kidding, I was 22
and dirt poor at the time) After being taught to play, and reading
through the collection of cards I was immediately intriqued by the mere
fact you did not need to be living of mommy and daddy, own a card store,
or an independantly wealthy single lifeless loser inorder to build
competitive decks in Jyhad. The mix of abilities between the clans (and
later I discover by not limiting to clans but by focusing on discipline
combinations) allowed anyone with access to a collection of inexpensive
cards to create extremely competitive decks.

Another point I alluded to earlier, the cliche-ness of M:TG games really
iritated me. I was continually seeing the same decks winning over, and
over, and over.

Which leads me to the cliche vs. Cheese. Anyone can throw a couple dozen
Night Moves into a deck, toss in a crypt of vamps with cap less than 4,
all with obfs, and use the auspex or dominate you will inevitably end up
with for T-midirection / deflection. That's a no brainer. A drunken
monkey taught to play using sign language could make that deck (and it's
a damn good one too.) But who wants to sit down to coffee and apetizers
at the local restaurant with a group of freinds and throw down Nmoves
after endless Nmoves and bore your prey to death one by one. (My tone
here is jovial, not attacking before the flame wars start :) :) :))

It's Cliche, it's Status-Quo.. It's the Backstreet Boys of Jyhad deck
design. (Good analogy, the Backstreet Boys are worth millions of dollars
(a winning deck if you will) but they are dull, drab, boring, and
cliche').

So I propose that in lieu of calling decks Cheesy, perhaps we should use
the term Cliche as this is more appropriate and sounds less like
whining. After all I can see the point some are making that it sounds
like those of us who eschew cliche' decks are whinning because our
hoighty-toighty theme decks don't win. Which isn't my point at all. My
hoighty-toighty theme decks can, and *do* win quite frequently amongst
the group of players in this area (while half of the time my Grand Pred,
which I assume is your last predator, can oust me before I oust him, I
am usually one of the last 2 players out of 5 -8)

This also extends to my approach to many things. In my younger days I
held outright disdain for anything mainstream.. Now that I'm older and a
bit wiser I can more closely analyze the mainstream, and decide for
myself instead of just scoffing because everyone else embraced it.

As a final thought, it is always my goal to win a game. However winning
is never enough for me. I want to win with style, sometimes develop a
story, make references to the Vampire (tm) mythos, cover as many
contingincies as possible, and avoid being repetitve, boring, and most
of all....

Cliche'.

--David

What makes you think Peter isn't? I didn't see him saying anything like
that. What he's _saying_ is that winning has to be the major motivation
or the design of the game breaks down. This doesn't exclude other
motivations. Indeed, I expect that even the most competitive players -
if they're smart - will play some games with the intent not put out the
absolute greatest effort to win but to make choices based on the objective
of learning how different decks and tactics work. Meaning, instead of
making the choices they feel are the most optimal at any given moment,
they'll deliberately make different choices just to see what would happen
and how they work. But they're still choices intended, at heart, to
winning the game.

If you *don't* play the game with intent to win, OTOH, you likely screw
the game up beyond recognition. For instance, a player intent on totally
random actions or on being excused from the game in the shortest possible
time will benefit his preditor greatly and his prey (less so and only at
first) unfairly in comparison to the other players.

>Hey, I like winning, too, and again, I wasn't pushing for a malicious
>angle. But what I like even more is winning with style, which it
>seems you do, too.

Right. The problem is that appears you (at least at first) seemed to be
assuming that a person's position on cheese depends on what he wants out
of the game. That's not a very good assumption.

Fred

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
David wrote:
<<Even
at that, creative types are looking for a unique experience. In
addition to a competitive/effective deck selection, they would prefer
one free of the tired, unimaginative, same old s^*t >>

That is a fine motivation to have, but the way to go about fixing it is to come
up with a well defined set of rules, where in what is unacceptable is very cut
and dry, and then play in that environment.

As Fred and I have both pointed out in various places is that the biggest
problem with the "cheese deck" world view is that it is completely
undefined--what one player sees as horrible, booring, and unimaginitive,
another sees as very clever. Using some sort of poorly defined "cheese" concept
to harrass players out of playing decks that "you" think are "cheesy" gets no
one no where.

Why not develop are concrete defenition of what the problem is (i.e. what decks
are really bad and why) and invent rules to stop them? The main argument of the
4CL people is that they think playing 4CL prevents "cheesy" decks. They are
completely wrong, but that isn't the point--the point is that they are
attempting to quantify "cheesiness" and erradicate it. That is also what all
the rulings were for--in effect, to limit "cheesiness".

Just having one player say "hmm. That deck is cheesy. Don't play it any more,
knee biter..." fixes nothing. If somone wants to avoid cheese decks, impliment
rules to do so.

Messages.Author: Patrick Harris
Messages.Body:
[snip all]
I'm not sure where to put this, but I believe it belongs in this thread:

I believe that what make certain decks "cheese" to some people are the facts
that the decks are usually very easy to make and that the decks are usually
played by many players.

Take the standard Presence weenie bleed decks, for example. The deck is quite
simple to make, and many people play them. The reasons are that 1) most if not
all the cards required are easy to come by (not rare), 2) the deck can win in a
tournament setting and 3) people have to be prepared for it, or it will win
easily. There are others, I'm sure, but these are the main reasons I can think
of.

The problem I have with the deck is not so much the first two reasons I listed,
but rather the third. And why do people have to be prepared for this deck? I
don't think it's because of the deck's effectiveness. I think it's because the
deck is so widespread. If there weren't so many of these decks at every
tournament, I don't think the deck would be considered cheese at all.

For instance, if decks containing large vampires were the mainstay in tourneys
(rather than the weenie bleeds), I believe the weenie bleed decks would have a
hard time getting past their grand preys. Gaining one, and every once in a
while two, victory points per table usually doesn't get you to the finals. And
without the deck being the table sweeper that it can be now, I don't think it's
going to be considered cheese, nor would players have to be prepared for that
specific type of deck.

I think this all comes down to the metagame. If most of the people in an area
start using large vampires in a crypt, the weenie decks left will suffer. (And
I'm thinking about good decks using large vampires. Efficient decks that gain
blood while taking effective actions, etc. Having big vamps just to have big
vamps won't do it.) Same as if most people start playing Fortitude prevent
decks. The Potence combat decks will suffer. The problem for me is that the
weenie bleed deck isn't a metagame concept, but a "mega-game" concept. It's
everywhere, and you have to prepare for it. I guess I don't like that thought,
but I accept it.

All decks being equal, in both effectiveness and frequency, I believe there
would be far more deck styles viable in a tournament setting if the weenie bleed
decks weren't so prominent. It's hard to argue that belief though, as there are
no facts to back it up. I haven't seen or heard of a tournament where weenie
bleed was neither in force nor expected to be in force.

Personally, I can't argue much against so-called cheese decks. In my play
group, we like to go with more of a storytelling theme for our decks. VPs are
not as important as being the last man standing. So our decks tend to be more
towards surviving, but not necessarily to the point of walling up and just
outlasting, as that tends to get boring. But if I'm going to a tournament, I
put away those decks and bring the typical tournament decks. Sure, if everyone
was playing large vampire decks I'd bring those and play. But at a table where
I'm likely to see 2-3 weenie bleed decks, I wouldn't stand a chance with a large
crypt, and I know it. So those decks stay at home. I don't complain though,
because I know the setting when I go into a tournament. Would I like to see a
little more diversity in the sizes of the crypts in tourneys? Sure. There
aren't that many effective decks out there will large crypts. There are some, I
know. But not many.

Hmm... talk about rambling. Geez. I don't even know if I've made a point about
anything, or just stated an opinion (albeit a vague and lengthy one). Anyway,
there it is.

p.

> weenie Misdirect, for the same reasons. I can see, though, that they

> do have a negative effect on the level of creativity on a tournament
> level...

There seem to be (of course) several different meanings of "cheese"
being floated around on this thread (and other parallel threads).

Here "cheese" seems to be any strong deck that makes use of a single
strong card (Misdirection) too often. (different from what some others
are arguing about: decks that are too strong.)

And the argument is that, by trying to win with a strong deck, the
competitor has lessened the "quality" of the event by causing certain
(possibly novel but apparently weaker) decks not to be able to compete.

Whereas if he had played any equally strong deck that had some "style"
(whatever we can agree that that is), he would win equally as much
(and afford the novel-but-weaker decks the same odds as before), but now
the tourney environment would not be hampered by "cheese". Yet the
novel-but-weaker decks still lose.

Either the argument is that some decks are *overly* strong, "cheesy"
(monotonous) or not, or that cheese is simply boring, strong or not.

Your argument is directed against very strong decks, not cheesy decks
in general. This is a real concern *if* the very strong deck is overly
strong (working with some unbalanced card or combination of cards), in
which case the mechanic (card, combo, or rule) that allows the imbalance
should be examined (and corrected).

But to argue that strong-but-boring decks hur the tournament scene is
another story. The tournament environment is founded on the notion
of rewarding the strongest deck (as an extension of the foundation of
the rules in general). The players are expected to each play as strong
a deck as they (individually) can, and to play them as well as possible.
While a player can certainly experiment with novel cards, combos, and
strategies, it is understood that they are doing so to *improve* their
chances of winning - to find a better combo or strategy (in general,
of just for the current meta-game). They are not expected to do so just
to avoid being "cheesy".

Analogy: In chess, e2-e4 is typically viewed as a strong, if not the
strongest, opening move. Even in a chess tournament, however, you will
see players play other opening moves. The other moves are not played to
simply enhance the variety of the game for the opposing players - they are
played to win, either by catching the opponent ill-prepared to properly
respond to such a non-standard move, or simply because the other move is
viewed as a suitable strong move in and of itself. But, if you choose to
play e2-e4, (and even if, for example, you follow the four-knights opening
for many moves), or if your opponent responds to your non-standard move
with a strong move, certainly no one will complain about the "cheese"
involved. The object is to play to win.

To purposefully play a weak move just to avoid the monotony of playing your strongest move (rather than making a questionable move in the hopes of
bettering your position) would detract from the tournament as a whole.

In both VTES and chess, the object of playing in a tournament may well be
(and should be, IMHO) to have fun. But that goal is best achieved if *all*
of the participants play each game to the best of their abilities - using
whatever resources (time limits, misdirection, etc.) are allowed.

(Chess is just a hobby - forgive any errors in the above discourse on
the game - hopefully the point I was trying to make remains intact.)

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
R. David Zopf wrote:
>>Simple to state, but most likely impossible to actually implement.>>

True, on a grand scale. However, attempting to shame your opponents out of
playing "cheesy" decks is also impossible to actually impliment. As far as I
can tell, the whole purpose of deciding that some deck designs are "cheesy" is
to attempt to get your opponents to stop playing them--either by mocking them
out of doing so, convincing the table to gang up on them for playing such a
cheesy deck, or using constant peer pressure to prevent them from playing such
decks. This is a farily common occurance, and my point is that it is a dumb
thing to try and do. If a given group of players has a problem with "cheesy"
decks, they should come up with quantifyable, easily definable rules to prevent
such decks from being played (as house rules, for instance). This is much more
effective than yelling at Steve because he is playing a deck that you don't
like.

>>Using rules structure to prohibit certain deck strategies isn't such a great
idea, IMHO.>>

But using peer pressure, out of game abuse, mocking, and complaint is a good
way to prohibit certain deck strategies (as is the aim of "cheese"
determination)?

>>I agree with limitations on overpowered cards (RtI, Mind Rape,
etc.), but to start messing with tournament rules in a way that prohibits a
specific deck concept from working is asking for trouble.>>

I agree 100%. But then I'm also not defending the concept that "cheese" decks
"ruin" tournaments.

>>A house rule would be about the only way of making such a tactic work. In
effect, thats what the peer pressure route to limiting cliche' decks is, an
unofficial or informal house rule. For me, that's where it should be. But
don't think I won't rag on someone for playing>>

But the problem with "unofficial" or "informal" house rules is that they are
inconsistient, don't apply to all players equally, and generally benefit the
players with the most pursuasive personalities more than anyone else. As this
tends to piss people off (as well as being a completely arbitrary factor in a
game with very well defined rules), and rarely ever seems to actually prevent
people from playing such "cheesy" decks, why not come up with "official" or
"formal" rules for a given play group that are easily defined, easily adhered
to, and easily quantified?

>>That was what I was getting at with the suggestion of evolution through
expansion. We haven't had a new influx of cards since '95-96, and it would
certainly be neat to have a few more tools that would do an efficient job of
supressing weenie tap and bleed deck styles, but we can't expect that.>>

Ahh. If only the world were kind :-)

>>Even so, I still resist the idea of implementing formal rules to get the same
effect. It would involve no small amount of rules manipulation. I think
that the limited formats (draft and sealed) are where people on opposite
sides of this argument will really find their common ground, as it makes
focused decks like weenie tap-n-bleed a non-issue.>>

I don't quite understand the logic of resisting formal house rules to prevent
"cheesiness" if a given group is putting effort into shaming people out of
playing "cheesy" decks. If a player is likely to get mocked for playing what
other people consider "cheesy" (which a nebulous concept, at best), how does he
know what to avoid doing? How does he know if a given deck has crossed the line
from "acceptable" to "cheesy"? If you are going to want to avoid "cheesy"
decks, why not just come up with rules to do so. so every one knows what to
expect.

You have made some very good Points!

First:
Tap and bleed, and for that matter sneak and bleed, decks use mostly common
cards. Therefore a player can create a good tourney deck with a fairly
small collection of cards. It is also a well known deck archetype. This
explains some of its it's popular appeal. You see a player (good or bad,
experienced or inexperienced) can quickly slap to together a workable very
focused deck. Yes there is some skill in making and playing a good T&B, but
I am speaking generally.

On the other extreme you have Peter's "The Nosferatu Hate You", Mk. IV. A
great deck. But this deck has something like 30 rare cards and takes a lot
of play time to master. Who to go after, who to threaten etc...(By the way
this deck is awesome! "behind you" just rocks!) I hope you see my point,
or should I say Patrick's.

Second:
If it is a very popular deck you see often at tourneys. Then as you state
we have the bases for a "mega game" discussion. Which by the way is a sign
of the maturity of the game.

It is hard to evolve a CCG because of the fact that it is collectable, and
is constantly coming out with new cards. But as we all know this is not the
case with Jyhad. So with out new cards we have a set number of variables.
This means deck discussion takes (or has already taken) on very different
connotation. With fixed variables there are only so many different card
combinations. In this environment certain card combinations (i.e. decks)
will float to the top. An even better bases for a mega-game discussion. To
some degree we have been talking on this level for some time. Maybe I am
just slow, but this dose change how I think about the game and the decks I
will play. More later....

Now I have a question. What deck types are archetypes? By this I mean
viable mega-game decks. T&B and S&B are two that I think we can all agree
on. Any others? Thoughts????? People talk to me.

In article <37BE3C6D...@sonic.net>,
David Bowsky <bag...@sonic.net> wrote:
[snip]

> I find it interesting that the term "Cliche' deck" is used above, and
> perhaps we should substitute Cliche for Cheese as it seems more
> appropriate. <<more on this below>>

I think this does seem to be a large part of the anti-
cheese mentality: that people shouldn't play 'boring'
decks. Usually they seem to mean 'boring but effective'
decks, but the 'boring' seems to be the main objection.

To me, it seems that these 'boring but effective' decks
are nothing but a basic vocabulary of good Jyhad tournament
deck design. People who are new to tournaments often play
Malk stealth&bleed decks in them, because the cards
needed to make them are relatively common, and the deck
concept is straightforward. They not infrequently play
weenie bleed decks or presence vote decks for the same
reason. Nowadays they may even play potence rush combat
decks, because the deck concept is well-understood and
well-described (at least on the net). All of these deck
types can now be described by experienced players as
'cheesy' or 'boring'. But they are only 'boring' if
you've already played them/played against them a hundred
times. If you're new to the game, or to tournaments, they
may still be fun to play. Even if you *have* played them
a hundred times, you may still enjoy the strategic interaction
at any given table - the general play of your deck and
all the others may be clear from the outset, but the actual
playing of the game can still be unique.

So, for me, no deck deserves to be ostracized or ridiculed
for being 'cheesy' or 'boring'. I may not think I would
enjoy playing the deck, but I don't consider it necessary
to discourage the person who is playing it from having a
good time if it's what s/he likes. I am certainly more
entertained by seeing some crazy concept deck that would
never have occurred to me than by seeing 'yet another
weenie dominate/misdirection deck', but in a tournament
it is the strategic interaction that I've come for, not
the novelty value.

Josh

besides, a novelty deck is only funny once
(just ask anyone who's played against cryptic
mission/society of leopold decks)
